keyVerseText: And Lot lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered every where, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, even as the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, as thou comest unto Zoar.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מַשְׁקֶה (mashqeh) derives from the root שָׁקָה (shaqah), which means to cause to drink, to water, or to irrigate. This root conveys the action of providing drink or moisture, whether to people, animals, or land. Thus, the literal sense of מַשְׁקֶה is connected to the act of giving drink or watering, extending metaphorically to roles and places associated with nourishment and refreshment, such as a butler or a well-watered region.
usageInScripture: The word מַשְׁקֶה appears 19 times in the Hebrew Bible with a range of related meanings. It is used to denote a butler or cupbearer, emphasizing the office responsible for giving drink, as well as the act of drinking or the vessels used for drinking. Additionally, it describes well-watered or irrigated land, highlighting fertility and abundance. This variety in translation—from 'unto his butlership' to 'that it was well watered'—shows a consistent theme of provision and refreshment, whether in human service or agricultural blessing.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מַשְׁקֶה enriches our appreciation of God’s provision in Scripture. The image of causing to drink or watering points to God as the ultimate source of spiritual nourishment and life-sustaining refreshment. The role of the butler as one who serves drink can be seen as a type of faithful servant who ministers God’s blessings to others. Moreover, the reference to well-watered land symbolizes the flourishing life that comes from God’s blessing. This word reminds believers that just as water sustains physical life, God’s grace sustains spiritual life, making Him the true source of refreshment and abundance.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 13:10 describes Lot looking over the plain of Jordan and noting that it was 'well watered everywhere,' using the concept of מַשְׁקֶה to emphasize the land’s fertility and blessing. This verse highlights the contrast between the lush provision of the land and the judgment that would soon come upon Sodom and Gomorrah. The word מַשְׁקֶה here enriches the imagery of God’s provision and blessing, reminding readers that just as the land was abundantly watered, so God’s care and provision are evident in the blessings He bestows.
